title: Senate Fails Clarity Act Cloture Vote on September 15; Ethics Divide Kills Crypto Bill
dek: The U.S. Senate failed to advance the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act on September 15, 2026, after a cloture motion fell short of 60 votes. Seven Democratic negotiators who shaped the bill voted against it, citing ethics provisions they said were too weak to prevent Trump and his appointees from profiting off crypto ventures while overseeing the industry.
author: Crypto Cronkite
key_fact: The cloture vote failed, blocking the measure that would have split crypto oversight between the SEC and CFTC.
bottom_line: Democrats held enough votes to block cloture and signaled they will not support ethics language that leaves Trump's crypto interests unregulated. Revival would require reopening ethics provisions Republicans had presented as final, a process staff-level talks have already failed to resolve. The next move belongs to Republicans, who must decide whether to accept stronger enforcement mechanisms or allow the bill to remain dead through the remainder of the 2026 session.
body: The U.S. Senate blocked the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act on September 15, 2026, when a cloture motion to begin floor debate fell short of the required 60 votes. The measure, championed by Republicans and the crypto industry as the first comprehensive federal framework for digital assets, died over unresolved ethics provisions governing financial interests held by President Trump and his administration.

Seven Democratic senators who had spent months negotiating the bill voted against the cloture motion: Kirsten Gillibrand, Mark Warner, Cory Booker, Raphael Warnock, Ruben Gallego, Angela Alsobrooks, and Catherine Cortez Masto. Their opposition reflected a fundamental disagreement over whether final ethics language adequately prevented sitting officials from profiting from crypto ventures while overseeing crypto regulation.

The breakdown centered on a set of ethics provisions Republicans released late Sunday night, negotiated with the White House and framed as the final compromise. Sen. Elissa Slotkin said the restrictions on Trump's financial interests remained inadequate, stating the ethics provisions were "simply too thin." Slotkin raised additional concerns about enforcement capacity and national security, questioning whether the Commodity Futures Trading Commission had sufficient staffing to enforce the framework's standards against money laundering tied to terrorist groups, North Korea, and Iran.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren, ranking member of the Senate Banking Committee, argued in prepared remarks that the ethics text created loopholes allowing Trump to continue profiting from his crypto ventures and create new ones. According to Warren's statement, the bill gave Trump's appointees at the Attorney General's office and the Office of Government Ethics the power to waive ethics restrictions entirely, rendering them unenforceable against the President. Warren stated: "We need crypto regulation, but not a crypto bill written by the crypto industry to benefit only the most extreme voices in the crypto industry at the expense of our national security, our economic stability, and to help the most corrupt President in the history of the United States make himself even richer."

The final text, released by Republicans, incorporated 635 pages of amendments and claimed to include 126 substantive changes Democrats requested. According to CryptoSlate's reporting, Senate staff met in the Capitol hideaway office of Sen. Thom Tillis to discuss possible final changes, but staff working for Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott later ended the talks without an agreement. Sen. Bernie Sanders told the chamber that crypto billionaires had spent nearly $300 million on midterm elections while Trump and his family had collected more than $1.4 billion from crypto-related ventures in 2025 alone, per Warren's statement.

The collapse took immediate effect in crypto asset markets. Coinbase, Circle, and Galaxy led a broad decline in crypto-focused stocks, per CoinDesk's reporting. The bill's failure returned crypto regulation to legislative limbo, with no clear timeline for reviving efforts that have consumed Senate energy since late 2024.

The Clarity Act, as designed, would have split oversight between the SEC and CFTC, assigning tokens classed as commodities to the futures regulator and those meeting securities definitions to the SEC. The structure was intended to reduce legal ambiguity that has locked the industry in a prolonged cycle of enforcement and litigation.
